doc.title: Vi Redd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999

title: Influences: Charlie Parker, Sonny Stitt and playing like singing
summary: She saw Bird humbly asking for his union card at 767, and credits her aunt's lyric-learning rule and Buddy Collette's Sinatra compliment.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Who do you name as your basic influences or people that you looked up to on the saxophone?

Well you can’t speak about the alto saxophone unless you say Charlie Parker, Bird Parker. At the time when — I saw Bird one time, in that 767 when he came in there when he had some union problem see. You know he wasn’t concerned about a union card or whatever, but he came to Los Angeles and he didn’t have his union card, and the Mr. Elmer Thane said, “Oh you can’t play” blah-blah-blah-blah-blah. And he came and I was working there that day, and he asked Florence, “Florence, please ask Thane to give me my card.” He was so humble. That’s the only time I ever saw him. And he had such a humble spirit. And I said, “Florence, is that Bird? Is that Yardbird?” She said, “Yeah, that’s Bird.” But I never got a chance to hear him play, you know? I never got a chance. But in some strange way his music was in the air, and it influenced me and so many others. And of course I liked — who was this guy, Tab Smith?

And Sonny Stitt was a good player. I got to know him later on. We played together one night in Chicago in the 70s. But I don’t know, music, who influenced me, the whole nine yards, it just seems like osmosis. It’s just I can’t say that I tried to play like somebody or I tried to sing like somebody, it was just whatever I did it just happened sort of. I like vocalists very much, because my aunt used to make us, when we had to play a solo, she used to make us learn the lyrics to the song. And she’d say, “You’re supposed to play like you’re singing.” So I always did. I liked Billy Eckstine very much and I hope that explains it.
And that’s good advice about knowing the lyrics to a song.

Right. And Buddy Collette paid me a wonderful compliment once. My dad gave him his first job. And he told me when I was playing one time, he says, “You know what? You play a melody just like Frank Sinatra sings.” And I said, “Oh really?” And he said, “You’re singing all the time.” And I said yeah, well my aunt made us learn, if you’re going to play [sings] In my solitude you haunt me. We had to learn that. We had to learn. And I said I don’t know it, I just want to play it, and she’d say, “No, learn all those lyrics.” And I think that’s good for instrumentalists.
